lead: A signal is a physical quantity that changes to carry information: voltage on a copper pair, light in a fibre, a radio wave in air. Analog signals change smoothly; digital signals jump between fixed levels. Three numbers — amplitude, frequency and phase — describe a sine wave completely. This chapter fixes those numbers with units, separates bit rate from baud rate, and ends at the sampling rule that turns one voice call into 64 kbit/s — the arithmetic behind every telephone link and every UPI payment that rides on one.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for where the physical layer sits under the data link layer.

blocks.text: A signal is a quantity that carries information by changing with time: voltage in volts, current in amperes, light power in watts. A periodic signal repeats exactly after a fixed interval; one repetition is one cycle. An aperiodic signal, such as a burst of noise, never repeats.

Four numbers describe a sine wave. Amplitude A is the peak value in volts, measured from zero. Period T is the time for one full cycle, in seconds. Frequency f is the number of cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Phase φ is the shift from a chosen starting point, in degrees or radians, where 360° is one full cycle. A 250 Hz tone has T = 4 ms; doubling f halves T.

blocks.where: f is frequency in hertz, T is period in seconds, λ is wavelength in metres, v is the signal speed in that medium in m/s. Free space gives v ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; a copper cable gives about 2 × 10⁸ m/s.

sections.h3: Analog versus digital, bit rate versus baud rate

blocks.text: An analog signal takes every value in a range, smoothly: a microphone voltage follows the speaker's voice exactly. A digital signal allows only a fixed set of values, called levels — usually two, high and low, written 1 and 0.

For a digital signal the bit interval is the time one bit occupies, in seconds, and the bit rate is bits per second: bit rate = 1/bit interval. Baud rate counts signal changes, or symbols, per second. When one symbol carries one bit the two rates are equal; when a symbol carries n bits, bit rate = n × baud rate.
In the figure the sine has T = 4 ms, so f = 250 Hz. The square wave changes level every 1 ms, so each bit lasts 1 ms and the bit rate is 1000 bit/s.

items: Baseband: the signal occupies frequencies from zero upward, as on a direct wire link.
Passband: the signal is shifted onto a carrier band away from zero, as radio and cable TV need.

blocks.text: Sampling theorem: a signal whose highest frequency is f_max is completely described by samples taken at f_s ≥ 2 f_max, where f_s is the number of samples per second. Sample slower and the shifted copies overlap — aliasing — and the original cannot be rebuilt.
PCM (pulse code modulation) turns samples into bits in three steps.

items: Sample the analog signal f_s times per second.
Quantise each sample to the nearest of a fixed set of levels, say 256 levels.
Encode each level as a fixed-length binary code — 8 bits for 256 levels.

blocks.text: Telephone voice is limited to 4 kHz, so f_s = 8000 samples/s; with 8 bits per sample the rate is 8000 × 8 = 64 000 bit/s = 64 kbit/s, one voice channel. Fewer bits per sample means coarser levels and more quantisation noise, which is why 8 bits is the usual compromise.

figure.caption: The analog signal repeats every 4 ms, so f = 250 Hz and λ = 2 × 10⁸ ÷ 250 = 800 km in the cable. The digital signal holds each bit for 0.25 µs, so its bit rate is 1 ÷ 0.25 µs = 4 Mbit/s.

spec.aria: Top, two cycles of a sine over 8 ms with one period of 4 ms marked; bottom, a two-level digital wave of eight bits with one bit interval of 0.25 µs marked.

examples.question: An analog signal completes 50 full cycles in 0.2 s and travels in a cable at 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Find its frequency, its period and its wavelength. A digital signal then sends 1000 bits in 0.25 ms; find its bit rate and bit interval.
steps: Frequency is cycles divided by time: f = 50 ÷ 0.2 s = 250 Hz.
Period is the inverse: T = 1 ÷ 250 Hz = 0.004 s = 4 ms.
Wavelength uses the speed in the cable: λ = (2 × 10⁸ m/s) ÷ 250 Hz = 800000 m = 800 km.
Bit interval = 0.25 ms ÷ 1000 bits = 2.5e-07 s = 0.25 µs.
Bit rate = 1 ÷ (2.5e-07 s) = 4000000 bit/s = 4 Mbit/s, which is also 1000 ÷ (0.25 × 10⁻³ s).
examples.answer: f = 250 Hz, T = 0.004 s (4 ms), λ = 800000 m (800 km), bit rate = 4000000 bit/s (4 Mbit/s) and bit interval = 2.5e-07 s (0.25 µs).
examples.check:
f = 50/0.2
T = 1/f
lam = 2e8/f
bits = 1000
dur = 0.25e-3
bit_rate = bits/dur
bit_interval = dur/bits
print(f)
print(T)
print(lam)
print(bit_rate)
print(bit_interval)

traps: Putting milliseconds into f = 1/T without converting: T = 4 ms gives f = 1 ÷ 0.004 s = 250 Hz, not 4 Hz.
Swapping bit rate and baud rate. They are equal only when one symbol carries exactly one bit.
Using the free-space speed to find wavelength in a cable; λ = v/f needs the speed in that medium.
Treating f_s = 2 f_max as a safe margin. It is the bare limit; practical systems sample above it.
Reading 'period = 0.2 s' and writing frequency = 0.2 Hz. Frequency is cycles ÷ time.

quiz.q: Define bit interval and bit rate, with units.
quiz.a: Bit interval: seconds per bit. Bit rate: bits per second = 1/bit interval.
A signal whose highest frequency is f_max is fully described by samples at f_s ≥ 2 f_max.

quiz.q: Why does a digital signal tolerate noise better than an analog one?
quiz.a: The receiver only has to choose among a few levels, so small added noise does not change the value it recovers.

quiz.q: A sine wave has T = 0.5 ms. Find its frequency.
A modem sends 4 × 10⁶ symbols per second, each symbol carrying 3 bits. Find the baud rate and the bit rate.
quiz.a: Baud rate = 4 × 10⁶ baud. Bit rate = 3 × 4 × 10⁶ = 12 Mbit/s.

quiz.q: A 6 kHz-bandlimited signal is sampled at 10 000 samples/s. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: 10 000 < 2 × 6000 = 12 000, so the theorem is violated: aliasing folds frequencies above 5 kHz onto lower ones and they cannot be recovered.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every mobile call is PCM inside the network: 8000 samples/s, 8 bits, 64 kbit/s, then compressed by codecs such as AMR to fit a radio channel. Software-defined radio samples right at the antenna, and the sampling theorem decides how fast that ADC must be. Search next: Nyquist–Shannon sampling, aliasing, quantisation noise, and companding with μ-law and A-law.
